passage: On the balcony of their Nashik flat, Omkar, five, frowned at his elephant jigsaw. Two pieces were left, and neither would fit. His big brother Tushar reached over. "Here, it goes..." "Don't tell me!" Omkar covered the gap with both hands. "Okay, okay." Tushar sat back. "Just... look at the corner." Omkar looked. The piece with the flat edge. He turned it, tried the corner, and it clicked. "I did it myself!" he announced. Tushar grinned and didn't say a word.

qa.q: How many pieces were left in Omkar's jigsaw?
qa.a: Two pieces.

qa.q: Why did Omkar cover the gap with both hands?
qa.a: He wanted to solve it himself and was worried Tushar would give away the answer.

qa.q: Which choice did Tushar make that helped Omkar most?
qa.a: He held back the answer and gave only a nudge, to look at the corner, so Omkar could finish it himself.

qa.q: Why might Tushar grin without saying a word?
qa.a: Tushar knew his hint helped but let Omkar keep the pride of doing it himself.

grounding: A five-year-old stuck on a jigsaw refuses the answer, accepts a nudge about the corner from his brother, and owns the win.

passage: "Ammi, the boat won't come!" Kiran pushed the wooden triangles around the mat. "Can I help?" asked Salma. "No! Don't tell me." "All right. A tiny clue?" Kiran squinted. "A tiny one. Not the answer." "The big triangle wants to be the sail." Kiran grabbed the big triangle and stood it up. "Like this?" "Hmm, what do you think?" He turned it once, then again. The sail fitted over the square. "The boat came! I made it!" "You did. Clue only." "Only a tiny clue," Kiran agreed, very serious.

qa.q: What did Salma's clue say about the big triangle?
qa.a: The big triangle wants to be the sail.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when he said 'Don't tell me'?
qa.a: He was stuck and a bit frustrated, but he wanted the win to be his own.

qa.q: What choice did Salma make when Kiran refused help, and why did it work?
qa.a: She offered a tiny clue instead of the answer, which Kiran could accept, so he still built the boat himself.

qa.q: Why might Salma answer 'what do you think?' instead of 'yes'?
qa.a: Salma wanted Kiran to check the sail himself, so the last step and the pride stayed his.

grounding: A young child stuck on a shape puzzle refuses the answer but accepts one small clue from his mother, keeping ownership of the win.

passage: Class note, Sunflower group, Tuesday. Written by Hansa Ma'am. Santosh, five, spent twenty minutes on the thirty-piece farm puzzle today. When I came near he said, "Don't tell me! I know it." He didn't, yet: the cow's head was upside down. I asked only, "Which corner has the blue sky?" He looked, tried the top corner, and the cow sat right. Then he pushed me gently away. "Now go, Ma'am." I went. He finished it alone and showed everyone. I will keep my clues this small with him; the win clearly matters to him.

qa.q: How many pieces did the farm puzzle have?
qa.a: Thirty pieces.

qa.q: What was Santosh wanting when he said 'Now go, Ma'am'?
qa.a: He wanted to finish on his own and own the win, now that the small clue had got him unstuck.

qa.q: What does Hansa Ma'am plan for next time, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She plans to keep her clues this small, because a nudge lets Santosh stay in charge while still getting unstuck.

qa.q: How might it have felt for Santosh if Hansa Ma'am had simply fixed the cow's head?
qa.a: He might have felt his puzzle was taken over and lost the pride of showing everyone something he finished himself.

grounding: A teacher records how a five-year-old wanted no answer, accepted one clue about a corner, and then sent her away to finish alone.

passage:
At the village fair, Madhuri's Bua had bought her a wooden tractor puzzle. Five, and very serious, Madhuri sat on the charpai under the neem with nine pieces and a frown. The big wheel would not go anywhere.
Gurpreet, her older cousin, leaned over. "That one goes..."
"Don't tell me!" Madhuri hugged the board to her chest.
"Okay. Just one clue?"
A long pause. "Small clue."
"Wheels live at the bottom."
Madhuri turned the wheel, tried the bottom corner, and pushed. Click. "I did it by myself," she announced. Gurpreet only nodded.

qa.q: Where did Madhuri sit with the puzzle?
qa.a: She sat on the charpai under the neem.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri hug the board when Gurpreet leaned over?
qa.a: She wanted to solve it herself and was afraid Gurpreet would give away the answer.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet's clue the right kind of help?
qa.a: It only said wheels live at the bottom, so Madhuri still had to find the spot and push the piece in herself.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet feel when Madhuri announces she did it by herself?
qa.a: Gurpreet might feel quietly amused and pleased, knowing the clue helped but letting her keep the pride. 🙂

grounding: A five-year-old stuck on a puzzle refuses the answer, accepts a small clue about where the wheels go, and claims the win.

passage:
On a rainy Sunday in Lisbon, Lucia, five, knelt at the kitchen table with a picture puzzle: four rows, and every row needs one apple, one pear, one banana and one grape card. One square was left empty, and she had three cards in her fist, all wrong-looking.
"Want me to..." her grandmother Esther began, drying a pot.
"No! Don't say it!"
"I'll keep quiet." Esther waited. Lucia's lip wobbled.
"Maybe tell me a bit," Lucia said. "Not the card."
"Look at the row with no banana."
Lucia's finger crept along the row. Her eyes went wide. She slapped the banana down. "I got it!"

qa.q: Which city was Lucia in on the rainy Sunday?
qa.a: She was in Lisbon.

qa.q: What does Lucia's wobbling lip suggest before she asks for a bit of help?
qa.a: It suggests she felt confused and frustrated, but still wanted the win to be hers.

qa.q: Why was 'Look at the row with no banana' a good nudge?
qa.a: It pointed her eyes to the right place without naming the card, so she still worked out the answer herself.

qa.q: How might Esther have felt standing quietly with the pot in her hands?
qa.a: Probably tempted to help and a little tense, but trusting that Lucia would ask when she was ready.

grounding: A five-year-old stuck on a picture puzzle refuses the answer and accepts only a nudge about which row to look at.
